Cubbon Park - Established in 1870, this vibrant city park has walking paths, landscaped gardens & play areas. It is home to over 6000 trees across nearly 100 species.

A bench is a bench. It is also a roof - for the ants beneath it, for whatever waits out the rain under its slats. We walk a short stretch of the park and use LOKA to record the places other species actually use.

To a slender loris, this canopy isn't scenery—it's an overhead highway keeping it safely off the ground. The tangled, thin branches are made for its pincer grip to creep silently, while the leafy ceiling acts like a backlit screen at night, turning bugs into easy silhouettes to snatch. By day, that thick foliage hides sleeping spots from raptors, and the unbroken bark gives it a continuous path to leave scent marks and trace out its territory.

Perched within the quiet expanse of Omkar Hills, the Sri Matsya Narayana Temple serves as a focal point of the local Omkar Ashram. It is a rare space dedicated to the fish avatar of Vishnu, offering a contemplative atmosphere removed from the city's busy pace.

Photo: Gpkp, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

This place used to be empty and full of trees, inhabited only by the local residents. There was no traffic, and life was easier to navigate. However, now people struggle to cross the area, and the quality of the environment has deteriorated. The increase in population is primarily due to real estate development, as house rents are cheaper here, attracting migrants.

Housed within a 140-year-old post office, the Sandesh Museum of Communication traces the evolution of India's postal history and the varied modes of communication that once connected the nation. Since opening in 2019, the refurbished space serves as a quiet archive for the tools and stories of a bygone era.

Hebbal serves as a quiet witness to Bengaluru's ancient origins, with a history stretching back 1,300 years. Once marking the city's northern boundary, the area holds the Hebbal Kittaya Inscription and two other valuable inscriptions that anchor its epigraphic heritage, with two now preserved for future study.

Photo: Pluday (Udaya Kumar P L), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Embedded in the quiet history of North Bengaluru, Allalasandra inscriptions and hero stones serve as a five-hundred-year-old record of local land and faith. A 1544 inscription found here documents the formal donation of the village to the Allalanatha temple in Jakkur, marking the site as a living archive.

Photo: Many.​ways, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
